questions.q: Why does the password field in /etc/passwd just show an 'x' instead of a hash?
options: Because /etc/passwd is world-readable, so the actual hash is stored in /etc/shadow instead
Because the account has no password set
Because 'x' means the account is disabled
Because passwords are stored in /etc/group instead
questions.explain: /etc/passwd must be readable by every process to resolve UIDs to names, so storing a real password hash there would be a security risk. The hash lives in the root-only /etc/shadow file.

questions.q: In /etc/passwd, which field is the user's primary group?
questions.explain: The record is username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. The GID field sets the user's single primary group.

questions.q: What is the effect of running `sudo usermod -G monitoring newhire` (note: -G, not -aG) on a user who is already in the ops group?
options: It adds monitoring on top of ops, leaving both groups intact
It replaces the user's supplementary groups entirely, so they lose ops and end up only in monitoring
It does nothing because the user already has a primary group
It deletes the monitoring group if it already exists
questions.explain: -G without -a sets the supplementary group list from scratch, overwriting any existing memberships. -aG appends instead of replacing.

questions.q: Where are a group's supplementary (non-primary) members listed?
questions.explain: /etc/group lists each group's GID and a comma-separated list of supplementary members. Primary group membership is set in /etc/passwd instead.

questions.q: Which command shows a user's UID, primary GID, and every group they belong to in one line?
questions.explain: id prints uid=..., gid=... (primary), and groups=... (every group, primary and supplementary) for the specified user.
